Split Tot to Train/Test

The model is fitted on Train, and the generalization error is estimated on Test. In this example, Train is already defined in variable typ of the dataset, and Test is defined by the remaining samples. But Tot could also be split a posteriori, for instance by sampling (random, systematic or any other designs). See for instance functions samprand, sampsys, etc.

s = typ .== "train"
Xtrain = Xp[s, :] 
Ytrain = Y[s, :]
Xtest = rmrow(Xp, s)
Ytest = rmrow(Y, s)
ntrain = nro(Xtrain)
ntest = nro(Xtest)
ntot = ntrain + ntest
(ntot = ntot, ntrain, ntest)

(ntot = 178, ntrain = 115, ntest = 63)

Working response y

namy = names(Y)[1:3]
j = 2  
nam = namy[j]    # work on the j-th y-variable
ytrain = Ytrain[:, nam]
ytest = Ytest[:, nam] ;

Split Train to Cal/Val for model tuning

The training set (Train) is split to a calibration set (Cal) and a validation set (Val). A grid search is implemented by fitting the model on Cal and computing a validation error on Val.

The split Cal/Val can be built from different sampling designs, such as the examples (not exhaustive) given below.

pct = .3  # proportion of Train for Val
nval = round(Int, pct * ntrain)

34

  • (1) Random sampling:

s = samprand(ntrain, nval)

(train = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12  …  102, 103, 105, 106, 107, 109, 110, 112, 114, 115], test = [7, 11, 17, 20, 22, 27, 31, 32, 33, 35  …  78, 84, 88, 90, 99, 101, 104, 108, 111, 113])

  • (2) Or Kennard-Stone sampling (Warning: output train contains higher variability than output test, see function sampks):

#s = sampks(Xtrain, nval; metric = :eucl)

  • (3) Or duplex sampling:

#s = sampdp(Xtrain, nval)

  • (4) Or systematic sampling over variable y:

#s = sampsys(ytrain, nval)

Xcal = Xtrain[s.train, :]
ycal = ytrain[s.train]
Xval = Xtrain[s.test, :]
yval = ytrain[s.test]
ncal = ntrain - nval 
(ntot = ntot, ntrain, ncal, nval, ntest)

(ntot = 178, ntrain = 115, ncal = 81, nval = 34, ntest = 63)

Grid-search

The generic syntax to use function gridscore is to set all parameters of the grid in argument pars built with function mpar. But for LV-based functions (eg. plskern, kplsr, lwplsr, etc.) it is more efficient to set parameter nlv outside argument pars. This optimizes the computation time.

The same principle applies when defining parameter lb in ridge-based functions (rr, krr, etc.). To set parameter lb outside argument pars optimizes the computation time.

nlv = 0:20
model = plskern()
@head res = gridscore(model, Xcal, ycal, Xval, yval; score = rmsep, nlv)

... (21, 2)

plotgrid(res.nlv, res.y1; step = 2, xlabel = "Nb. LVs", ylabel = "RMSEP-Val").f

Naïve syntax (not efficient for computation time)

To set nlv in argument pars is strictly equivalent (gives the same results) but is less efficient for computation time. 

pars = mpar(nlv = 0:20)
model = plskern()
@head gridscore(model, Xcal, ycal, Xval, yval; score = rmsep, pars)

u = findall(res.y1 .== minimum(res.y1))[1]

Fit the optimal model on the whole Train set

model = plskern(nlv = res.nlv[u])
fit!(model, Xtrain, ytrain)
@head pred = predict(model, Xtest).pred

Plotting predictions vs. observed data

plotxy(pred, ytest; size = (500, 400), color = (:red, .5), bisect = true, title = "Test set - variable $nam", 
    xlabel = "Prediction", ylabel = "Observed").f

Additional parameters in the grid

If other parameters have to be defined in the grid, they must be set in argument pars built with function mpar, such as in the example below.

pars = mpar(scal = [:none; :std])
nlv = 0:20
model = plskern()
@head res = gridscore(model, Xcal, ycal, Xval, yval; score = rmsep, pars, nlv)
